newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Deregulation sparks U.S. utility mergers.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Deregulation sparks U.S. utility mergers.

text.p: Looming deregulation in the domestic electric utility industry sparked several major merger announcements in 1996, part of a restructuring expected to sweep away monopoly control of electric power grids.

Several neighboring electric utilities announced plans to combine their local systems, while some competing electric and gas utilities announced mergers to take advantage of synergies in operating overlapping electric and gas networks.

And in two groundbreaking deals, electric utilities eyeing the potential to build nationwide energy franchises linked up with major natural gas companies in mergers expected to lead to a consolidation of the electric and natural gas industries.

"I think the jury is out on whether these things are going to pay off," said William Wise, chairman of El Paso Energy Corp, which became a prime merger candidate this year with its acquisition of Tenneco Energy.

With about $25 billion in pending utility mergers awaiting federal approval, regulators with the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission this week adopted streamlined procedures for reviewing the announced deals and an expected wave of new mergers.

The commission's new guidelines were seen trimming the approval process to as little as five months -- down from as much as two years or more -- using a revised framework for guaging the impact of both utility-with-utility and utility-with-gas company mergers.

The streamlined merger-approval process was expected to be a catalyst for deals by companies waiting for the federal agency to signal its willingness to quickly review utility combinations, analysts said.

"One of the things that has kept the pace relatively slow is the number or regulatory hurdles these deals have to go through," said Christopher Lowe, a banker with Chase Manhattan Bank's global power and environmental group.

Nine electric utility merger applications are pending with federal regulators, including Baltimore Gas and Electric Co with Potomac Electric Power Co, IES Utilities with Wisconsin Power and Light, Northern States Power Co with Wisconsin Electric Power.

In Texas, companies controlling overlapping electric and gas utilities -- Houston Industries Inc and NorAm Energy Corp in Houston and Texas Utilities and ENSERCH Corp in Dallas -- announced merger plans to take advantage of synergies and build their respective power-marketing operations.
And Houston natural gas companies Enron Corp and PanEnergy Corp broke new ground with plans to merge with electric utilities in bids to form national energy franchises.

Enron was first out of the blocks with its $3.2 billion merger with Portland General Corp, a capacity-short Oregon utility that shares Enron's philosophy of building a national electric and gas retail franchise.

That deal was quickly followed by the pending $7.7 billion merger of Duke Power Co and PanEnergy, which is one of the country's largest natural gas gatherers and processors with 37,000 miles of gas pipelines.

"We are witnessing the birth of the energy services industry -- end-to-end service from the wellhead to the household, as well as energy management for industrial companies," said U.S. Trust energy analyst Michael Hoover, who sees a handful of megamarketers emerging in the years ahead.
The short list of merger candidates among the nation's largest natural gas pipeline and marketing companies includes Williams Cos Inc, NGC Corp and Houston-based El Paso Energy.

El Paso Energy's Wise in a recent interview was cagey about the Houston company's plans to seek a suitor. But he left little doubt consolidation was the name of the game for the electric and gas industries, and he would be a player.

"I don't think there's any doubt that (consolidation) is the future for our industry and, I think, for the electric industry as well," Wise said. "I'm very excited about what role we're going to play."
